source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/CarhartHarris_2018_ImportanceOfContext.pdf, online-first version paginated 1-7 (anchors cite 'PDF p. N'). All running text read from the extracted text layer; pages 2-5 also read on 150-dpi renders and Figure 3 on a 300-dpi render of p. 5, where every coefficient and p value was checked. No supplement.

claims.overstatement: None for the part that comes from this source. The claim's description of it as an opinion piece previewing preliminary models in one figure, without methods, of what appears to be an earlier cut of the same survey, and its decision not to use its figures, matches what the paper shows; the overlap with Haijen is the editors' inference and is hedged as such ('appears to be').
claims.note: The paper gives no measures, sample description, model type or intervals, so nothing beyond the figure can be checked here. That the three predictors were rated before the drug is an inference from the item wording ('the upcoming experience') in the Figure 3 legend, not a stated measurement time.

anchors.locator: Figure 3, lower model (read on a 300-dpi render)
anchors.extracted: Factors which, if lacking, predict a challenging experience: readiness beta -0.46 (p < 0.01), intention -0.25 (p = 0.02), trust -0.37 (p < 0.01); challenging experience to well-being at 2 weeks beta -1.12 (p < 0.005). Full lines mark significant paths. No n per model, no intervals, no model type.

Two models from a web survey in 266 participants who completed surveys at four time points (1 week before, 1 day before, 1 day after, 2 weeks after a specific psychedelic experience). Readiness = 4 items (e.g. ready to surrender, open to the upcoming experience); intention = 2 items (clear intention; strong expectations for the upcoming experience); trust = 2 items on the relationship with the group/people present and the main person looking after the participant. The legend says the study will be reported more fully in forthcoming publications.

The preliminary results are referred to a forthcoming publication for a fuller account of the study's methods and results; model 1 is described as showing readiness, clear intention, therapeutic setting and higher dose predicting a 'peak' experience, and model 2 as showing the same factors plus trust protecting against a challenging one. The authors add that higher doses did not strongly predict challenging experiences in this sample and that it is probably biased (prior experience with and positive attitudes towards psychedelics).

claims.overstatement: None. 'How it was recorded is not given' for the therapeutic-setting variable is correct: the paper never describes the measure.
claims.note: The claim's statement about controlled studies not having been done is the paper's own 2018 assertion and is reproduced accurately, including the exceptions (dose-response study, retrospective analyses, Ludwig et al. 1969).

anchors.locator: Figure 3, upper and lower models (300-dpi render)
anchors.extracted: Upper model: therapeutic setting beta 0.26 (p = 0.013), intention 0.26 (p < 0.01), drug dose 0.2 (p = 0.04), readiness 0.16 (p = 0.076, broken line) predicting a peak experience; peak experience to well-being beta 1.96 (p < 0.001). Lower model: trust beta -0.37 (p < 0.01) among the factors whose absence predicts a challenging experience.

anchors.locator: Left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page
anchors.extracted: Other than a dose-response study (Griffiths et al. 2011) and retrospective analyses (e.g. Studerus et al. 2012), controlled studies designed to isolate and test key contextual variables had not been carried out, apart from Ludwig et al. (1969); the authors ascribe this to the practical and ethical difficulty of providing a sub-optimal context at a full dose.

Despite its widespread adoption among psychedelic researchers, few controlled studies had been performed to test the assumed relationship between psychedelics and context (Ludwig et al., 1969 excepted); the group's own nearest tests were of music, autobiographical memory scripts and suggestibility.

266 participants completing all four surveys; trust is a 2-item score about the people who will be present or look after the person during the upcoming experience; preliminary, to be reported more fully elsewhere.

key_findings.note: p. 3 right column 1st paragraph and p. 4 left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page; both checked.
-0.46, -0.25, -0.37, -1.12 and their p values re-read; setting and dose are indeed absent from this model.
p. 2, right column: the trials paragraph is the 2nd and the sitters paragraph the 3rd paragraph starting in that column; locator verified on the render.

reporting_issues.note: Text p. 4 says the same factors plus trust protect against a challenging experience; Figure 3's lower model has only readiness, intention and trust.
Readiness p = 0.076, drawn with a broken line.
'Predicts a deflation of this effect' (p. 4, right column, 1st full paragraph) against 'a trend relationship' in the next paragraph, with p < 0.005 in the figure.
Kaelen et al., 2017 appears twice on p. 3; the reference list (p. 7) has Kaelen et al. 2015 and Kaelen et al. 2018 only.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist is the right instrument for an opinion piece (METHODS 5.3); overall 'high' is not less severe than the worst domain, and the three 'high' domains match what I read (no search, no appraisal of cited work, reliance on the group's own studies).

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits: the only data are a methods-free figure, and the running text overstates that figure in three places.

missed: Figure 3's coefficients are on two different scales (predictors 0.16 to 0.46, experience-to-well-being 1.96 and -1.12), which suggests that not all of them are standardized; worth recording beside the card's note that the coefficient type is unreported, because the well-being paths cannot be read as standardized betas.
